concepts.eliForgot: Running several self-attention processes side by side, each specializing in noticing a different kind of relationship, then combining their findings.
concepts.definition: Extends self-attention by letting the model focus on different types of relationships simultaneously. Each head has its own Q/K/V transformation matrices (initialized randomly, learned via backpropagation), computes attention independently, and outputs are concatenated. Improves expressiveness, contextual understanding, and performance; avoids symmetry so each head learns unique relationships.
concepts.example: Head 1 might focus on subject-verb relationships ("cat" → "sat"); Head 2 might focus on object-preposition relationships ("mat" → "on").

concepts.eliForgot: The full blueprint: an encoder that reads and understands the input, and a decoder that generates the output — both built from stacked attention layers.
concepts.definition: Key components: Input embeddings (convert tokens to dense vectors), Positional embeddings (add position information — since attention has no inherent sense of word order, e.g. "John saw the dog" vs. "The dog saw John"), Self-attention (focus on relevant parts of the sentence). Encoder processes input into a rich context-aware representation; Decoder generates output one token at a time using the encoded input and previously generated tokens. Encoder and decoder often do not share weights.
concepts.example: Encoding "Leaves fall from the oak tree" into embedding vectors, then decoding token-by-token into "Les feuilles tombent du chêne."

concepts.eliForgot: An encoder-only model that reads a sentence in both directions at once (not just left-to-right) so it deeply understands context before answering.
concepts.definition: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Bidirectional contextual understanding (e.g. distinguishes "bank" meanings using both left and right context). Trained via Masked Language Modeling (MLM — predict masked tokens, e.g. "The cat sat on the [MASK]") and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP). Architecture: BERT-Base (12 layers, 768 hidden units, 12 attention heads), BERT-Large (24 layers, 1024 hidden units, 16 attention heads). Fine-tuned by adding task-specific heads: classification head for text classification, output layer for QA span prediction, token classification head for NER. Encoder-only, focused exclusively on understanding tasks (classification, NER, extractive QA, text similarity).
concepts.example: Fine-tuning BERT for sentiment analysis: add a classification head on top of pretrained BERT and train on labeled review data.

concepts.eliForgot: A decoder-only model that can only look backward at what's already been written, and its whole job is predicting the next word.
concepts.definition: Generative Pretrained Transformer, developed by OpenAI. Decoder-only, consists only of decoder blocks, trained as a causal language model (predicts the next token given preceding tokens). Unidirectional attention (only looks at previous tokens). Each decoder layer contains: Self-Attention (Causal — focuses only on past tokens), Feed-Forward Network, Layer Normalization and Residual Connections (for training stability). Pre-trained on massive datasets (Wikipedia, books). Scales from GPT-2 (1.5B params) to GPT-3 (175B) to GPT-4. Strengths: causal attention for coherent generation, zero-shot/few-shot learning, multitasking (writing, translating, summarizing, coding) with one architecture.
concepts.example: Given "Once upon a", GPT predicts the next token, then the next, generating text left-to-right using only prior context.

concepts.eliForgot: An encoder-decoder model that treats literally every NLP task — translation, summarization, classification — as "turn this text into that text."
concepts.definition: Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer. Reframes every NLP task as a text-to-text problem, rather than having task-specific architectures. Pretrained via Span Corruption ("fill-in-the-blank" — mask random spans of text, model fills them in), similar in spirit to BERT's MLM. Scalable across sizes (T5-Small to T5-XXL). Supports few-shot/zero-shot learning with minimal fine-tuning. Ideal for sequence-to-sequence tasks: machine translation, summarization, question answering, text simplification.
concepts.example: Input: "The [MASK] is blue and [MASK] over the sea." Target: "sky stretches" — the span-corruption pretraining task.

concepts.eliForgot: One family only reads (BERT), one family only writes (GPT), and one family reads then writes (T5) — pick based on whether your task is understanding or generating.
concepts.definition: Encoder-Only (BERT): primary task = understanding text, bidirectional attention, stacked encoder layers, pretraining = masked language modeling, strength = contextual understanding. Decoder-Only (GPT): primary task = generating text, unidirectional/causal attention, stacked decoder layers, pretraining = causal language modeling, strength = fluent text generation. Encoder-Decoder (T5): sequence-to-sequence tasks, uses both encoder and decoder, ideal for transformation of one sequence into another.
concepts.example: Classification/QA → BERT. Open-ended generation/chat → GPT. Translation/summarization → T5.

concepts.eliForgot: Three ways to work with Claude, each one built because the last one wasn't enough: talk to it, hand it your files, or let it run code.
concepts.definition: The Claude product ecosystem organized as three layers of increasing autonomy: Chat (think with AI, one-off conversational tasks), Cowork (work with AI on local files across multi-step tasks), and Code (delegate to AI for system-level automation). Each layer exists because the previous one is inefficient for certain types of work.
concepts.example: Drafting a quick email → Chat. Building a formatted multi-file report from existing spreadsheets → Cowork. Automating a recurring data pipeline → Code.

concepts.term: AI as a Consultant (vs. AI for Workflows)
concepts.eliForgot: Sometimes AI is like a smart friend you ask one question; sometimes it's like a coworker who takes an entire project off your plate.
concepts.definition: A framing distinction between using AI for quick, one-off tasks with a clear start and end (consultant mode — you drive, AI assists) versus using AI to own multi-step professional workflows end-to-end (workflow/agentic mode).
concepts.example: Asking Claude to rewrite a paragraph = consultant. Asking Claude to gather data, analyze it, and produce a formatted report = workflow.

concepts.term: Why Chat Breaks Down for Multi-Step Work
concepts.eliForgot: A chat window forgets everything between sessions, so you end up doing all the gluing-together yourself.
concepts.definition: Four reasons pure chat interfaces struggle with multi-step professional work: fragmented interface (context doesn't carry across sessions), repeated context (re-explaining background every message), manual stitching (connecting outputs between messages by hand), and the user still owning coordination and execution.
concepts.example: Building a weekly report in Chat means you paste data in, get a paragraph back, then manually copy it into a document yourself for every section.

concepts.eliForgot: The classic back-and-forth: you ask, Claude answers, you decide what to do with it.
concepts.definition: The conversational layer of the Claude ecosystem — quick, text-based, one-off tasks where the user drives the conversation and Claude responds to prompts without maintaining a persistent task or files.
concepts.example: Asking Claude to summarize a pasted article or brainstorm campaign taglines.

concepts.eliForgot: Give Claude a task and your files, and it goes and does the work instead of just talking about it.
concepts.definition: The file-based collaboration layer of the Claude ecosystem. Claude reads, edits, and creates files directly, maintains context across multi-step tasks, and executes a defined task end-to-end rather than just responding to individual prompts.
concepts.example: Uploading five data files and asking Cowork to build a complete formatted report from them.

concepts.eliForgot: The layer where Claude stops working inside a chat window and starts operating your systems directly, with full autonomy on a defined task.
concepts.definition: The system-level automation layer of the Claude ecosystem. Claude uses code to operate in systems — connecting to data sources, running queries, and executing defined tasks with full autonomy, rather than working through a chat or file interface.
concepts.example: Claude Code connecting to a database, running queries, and fetching the latest numbers automatically for a report.

concepts.eliForgot: Just hand Claude the actual file — the screenshot, the spreadsheet, the PDF — instead of typing out a text description of it.
concepts.definition: Providing Claude with raw artifacts (documents, PDFs, images, spreadsheets, code files) directly rather than manually translating their content into text first. Reduces information loss and friction, and turns Claude into a working interface for real-world artifacts rather than just a chatbot.
concepts.example: Uploading a screenshot of a broken UI instead of describing the bug in a paragraph.

concepts.eliForgot: Three sizes of the same brand: a cheap fast one, a balanced everyday one, and an expensive deep-thinking one.
concepts.definition: The Claude model family, organized around a speed–cost–quality tradeoff. Haiku: fastest and cheapest, best for high-volume simple tasks (classification, extraction, routing). Sonnet: balanced speed/cost/quality, best for everyday business tasks (writing, data analysis, daily workflows). Opus: slowest and most expensive, best for complex reasoning, strategy, and long-form multi-step analysis.
concepts.example: Routing thousands of support tickets by category → Haiku. Drafting a weekly report → Sonnet. Multi-step pricing strategy analysis → Opus.

concepts.eliForgot: Extended Thinking is you telling Claude 'think hard for this long'; Adaptive Thinking is Claude deciding for itself how much thinking the problem needs.
concepts.definition: Two approaches to controlling Claude's reasoning depth. Extended Thinking: the user explicitly sets how much Claude should think, giving predictable token usage — best when you already know a problem needs deep analysis. Adaptive Thinking: Claude automatically scales its reasoning based on the complexity it detects, which is simpler for most everyday use cases.
concepts.example: A quick email reply needs minimal thinking; a pricing strategy decision benefits from deep, extended reasoning.

concepts.term: System Prompt Design (Role, Tone, Constraints, Format)
concepts.eliForgot: A system prompt is the job description you give Claude before the conversation starts, so it acts like a specialist instead of a generalist.
concepts.definition: Structuring a system prompt around four elements — Role (who Claude should be), Tone (how it should communicate), Constraints (what it should avoid), and Output Format (how the response should be structured). Clearly demarcated sections eliminate vagueness and force specificity, transforming Claude from a generalist into a clearly defined specialist.
concepts.example: "You are a compliance-focused financial analyst (Role). Write concisely and formally (Tone). Never speculate beyond the provided data (Constraints). Respond in a three-bullet summary (Format)."

concepts.eliForgot: Plug-ins that let Claude reach into your actual tools instead of just answering inside a chat box.
concepts.definition: Integrations that let Claude browse and interact with web content (Chrome), analyze and edit spreadsheet data (Excel), create and edit presentations (PowerPoint), and access messages and channels (Slack). Connectors enable real-time data access, cross-tool workflows, and direct file creation/editing rather than manual copy-paste.
concepts.example: Asking Claude to pull live figures from a connected Slack channel directly into an Excel report.

concepts.eliForgot: The six things that make Cowork feel like a coworker instead of a chatbot: it can touch your files, split up work, produce real documents, run on a schedule, remember the task, and package itself into reusable bundles.
concepts.definition: Six defining capabilities of Claude Cowork: Direct Local File Access (reads/writes local files, no manual uploads), Sub-Agent Coordination (breaks complex work into smaller parallel tasks), Professional Outputs (generates Excel, PowerPoint, and formatted documents), Scheduled Tasks (runs on demand or on a recurring cadence via /schedule), Context Continuity (remembers task, intermediate outputs, and direction across steps), and Plugins (bundles skills, connectors, and sub-agents for a role, team, or company).
concepts.example: A Cowork task that reads five local files in parallel, then saves an Excel dashboard and a Word memo to an output folder.

concepts.term: The Agentic Loop (Plan → Approve → Execute → Iterate)
concepts.eliForgot: The four-beat rhythm of working with an AI agent: it tells you the plan, you approve it, it does the work, then you both refine the result together.
concepts.definition: The core workflow pattern for agentic Cowork tasks. Plan: Claude reads context and announces what it will do. Approve: the human reviews the plan before Claude starts. Execute: Claude works — reading files, analyzing, generating. Iterate: the human reviews output, suggests refinements, and Claude adjusts. Analogous to delegating to a competent colleague: brief them, approve the approach, let them work, review the result.
concepts.example: Claude proposes an 8-step plan for a monthly report, waits for approval, executes all 8 steps, then revises the commentary after feedback.

concepts.term: Human Oversight in Cowork (Visible Reasoning, Approval Gates, Supervisor Role)
concepts.eliForgot: The three guardrails that keep an autonomous AI agent safe to use at work: you can always see its thinking, it asks before doing anything risky, and nothing ships without your sign-off.
concepts.definition: Three safety mechanisms that make agentic AI usable for professional work: Visible Reasoning (Claude shows its plan and thinking before and during tasks), Approval Gates (Claude asks before significant actions like creating files or modifying data), and the Supervisor role (Claude proposes, the human approves — nothing happens without sign-off).
concepts.example: Before overwriting a shared spreadsheet, Cowork pauses and asks for explicit approval.

concepts.eliForgot: Instead of retyping the same good prompt every time, you save the whole workflow once and just trigger it by name from then on.
concepts.definition: Deterministic, reusable workflow instructions that can be saved and triggered repeatedly, turning a one-off Cowork workflow into a repeatable, shareable playbook. Benefits: repeatability (consistent runs), output consistency (same quality every time), and team-wide usage (shared across a team). Represents a progression from CLAUDE.md (project-level context) to Skills (reusable across projects and teams).
concepts.example: Saving a validated 'monthly close pack' workflow as a Skill so any analyst on the team can trigger it identically next month.

concepts.eliForgot: A file that tells Claude the standing rules of a project once, so it doesn't need to be re-briefed every session.
concepts.definition: A persistent context file that loads automatically every Cowork session, containing information such as folder structure and naming conventions, KPI targets, flag thresholds, standing workflow steps, formatting rules, and output folder conventions — so Claude already knows the rules before a task begins.
concepts.example: A CLAUDE.md specifying 'CSAT < 80% = RED' means Claude flags that threshold automatically without being told each time.

concepts.eliForgot: For big jobs, Claude splits the work into smaller pieces and works on several of them at the same time instead of one at a time.
concepts.definition: A Cowork capability where complex tasks are broken into smaller sub-tasks and worked on as parallel workstreams rather than sequentially, enabling faster handling of multi-source tasks (e.g. reading several files at once).
concepts.example: Reading five separate source files in parallel instead of one after another before cross-referencing them.

concepts.eliForgot: A workflow counts as agentic when the AI does things on its own initiative — opens files, plans ahead, works in parallel, connects information across sources, and can be scheduled to repeat — not just when it answers a question.
concepts.definition: Behaviors that distinguish agentic execution from reactive chat assistance: no file upload needed (opens local files directly), automatic context loading (e.g. from CLAUDE.md), plan-before-act (announces the full plan before writing anything), parallel sub-agent work, cross-source synthesis (connecting insights across different files), and one-command recurrence (e.g. /schedule) that turns a one-off task into an autonomous recurring workflow.
concepts.example: In the Monthly Close Pack case study, Claude opens 5 local files, cross-references a CSV against an Excel cost overrun, and can be scheduled to rerun automatically next month.

concepts.term: The Two Failure Modes RAG Fixes
concepts.eliForgot: Generative-only models make things up or go stale; retrieval-only systems just dump a pile of links on you and make you do the reading.
concepts.definition: Generative-only models: lack up-to-date information (may answer recent events with outdated or refused answers), and hallucinate (produce plausible-sounding but incorrect or unverifiable information). Retrieval-only systems: lack synthesis (return multiple relevant sources without summarizing or interpreting them cohesively), and put the burden on the user to manually review and extract insights.
concepts.example: A generative-only model confidently misstates a recent event; a retrieval-only search engine returns five relevant articles and leaves you to read all of them.

concepts.eliForgot: The pre-RAG way of finding information: rank and fetch existing documents, but never write anything new.
concepts.definition: The era before RAG split into two separate lanes. Retrieval-only models find and rank existing content using methods like BM25, TF-IDF, and embedding-based retrieval, but cannot generate fluent new text. Generative-only models (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and other LLMs) generate fluent new text but cannot pull in live external information.
concepts.example: BM25 ranks documents by keyword overlap and term frequency, returning the most relevant existing pages instead of writing a new answer.

concepts.eliForgot: Reads a sentence in both directions at once, which makes it great at understanding meaning but bad at writing new sentences.
concepts.definition: Bidirectional contextual understanding (e.g. resolving "The bank is on the river" using context from both sides of the ambiguous word). Strengths: document ranking, named entity recognition, question answering, retrieving relevant information. Weaknesses: cannot generate fluent responses, lacks creativity and coherence as a writer.
concepts.example: BERT is well-suited to being the retriever half of a RAG pipeline, but not the half that drafts the final answer.

concepts.eliForgot: Writes fluent text one word after the next, but only from what it already knows, which is exactly why it hallucinates.
concepts.definition: Unidirectional language modeling: processes text left-to-right. Strengths: highly fluent, excels in content creation. Weaknesses: lacks real-time retrieval, prone to hallucinations.
concepts.example: GPT can write a polished paragraph about breach of contract, but without retrieval it may state an incorrect rule with total confidence.

concepts.eliForgot: RAG is what you get when you glue BERT's "find the right stuff" strength to GPT's "write it up well" strength. Same pattern as the RAG entry in Task-Flow: QA, but here framed as which model architecture does which job.
concepts.definition: RAG uses retrieval (BERT-like) to find relevant information and generation (GPT-like) to produce the response. Strengths: retrieves live and up-to-date data, generates coherent responses, and handles complex and context-dependent questions that neither approach handles alone.
concepts.example: Given "Does intent matter in a breach of contract?", RAG retrieves current legal sources and generates an answer grounded in them, rather than a fluent but possibly wrong GPT-only guess.

concepts.eliForgot: Turn the question into numbers, go fetch the matching chunks of text, then hand those chunks to the LLM so it can write the answer.
concepts.definition: Text-based query → encoding → retrieve relevant text chunks → large language model generates an answer using the retrieved chunks as context. Common use cases: document Q&A, code-based search, knowledge assistants.
concepts.example: A user asks a knowledge assistant a product question; the pipeline encodes the query, retrieves the matching manual sections, and the LLM writes the answer from those sections.

concepts.eliForgot: Old-school search hands you a ranked list of pages and hopes the keywords line up; generative search actually understands the question and writes you an answer with sources.
concepts.definition: Traditional search lacks context and relies on keyword-based (SEO-influenced) ranking, correcting for this mainly through search-engine algorithms. Generative search has context to improve the quality of search, avoids keyword-based SEO optimization, and is more accurate and relevant — and can provide sourcing for its answers.
concepts.example: Searching "Which planet in the solar system has the most moons?" on generative search returns a direct, sourced answer instead of a list of pages to click through.

concepts.eliForgot: The four reasons RAG earns its place over either approach alone.
concepts.definition: Contextual accuracy (answers grounded in retrieved context), factual grounding (reduces hallucination by citing real retrieved data), scalability (new information can be added to the retrieval source without retraining the model), and customizability (retrieval source can be swapped or scoped per use case, e.g. a company's own documents).
concepts.example: A customer support bot stays current by updating its retrieval index with new help-center articles, with no model retraining required.

concepts.eliForgot: A ready-made toolkit for grading your RAG system on two separate report cards: did it find the right stuff, and did it write a good answer from it.
concepts.definition: An open-source framework (GitHub, Docs) that provides the necessary ingredients to evaluate a RAG pipeline at the component level, rather than only judging the final output as a whole.
concepts.example: Running RAGAs on a support-bot pipeline surfaces separately whether the retriever pulled the right documents and whether the generator used them well.

concepts.eliForgot: One job is fetching the right context; the other job is writing a good answer from that context — and they can each fail independently.
concepts.definition: In RAGAs' component-level view of a RAG pipeline: the Retriever Component retrieves additional context from an external database for the LLM to use in answering the query. The Generator Component generates an answer based on a prompt that has been augmented with the retrieved information.
concepts.example: A RAG system can have a strong generator but a weak retriever (fluent answer, wrong source) — evaluating the two components separately catches that.

concepts.eliForgot: If your RAG answers aren't good enough, there are three different places to intervene: what you're searching over, how you search it, or how you ask.
concepts.definition: RAG frequently needs optimization to best meet user needs. Three primary ways to augment it: transform the data (change what's indexed/how it's chunked), transform the retrieval (change how documents are found/ranked), and transform the query (rewrite or expand the user's query before retrieval). Being aware of how users actually interact with the system reveals the best avenues for augmentation.
concepts.example: If users' questions are vague, query transformation (rewriting the query before retrieval) may fix more errors than reindexing the data.

concepts.eliForgot: RAG that can dig up a diagram or photo, not just paragraphs of text, so it can actually answer questions that live in a picture.
concepts.definition: A RAG system that can access and reason over both textual and visual data, combining text and images in a unified retrieval process and generating grounded, context-rich answers. Addresses the limitation of text-only RAG: relevant information often lives in a diagram, image, or schematic. High-impact fields: manufacturing, medicine, aerospace, architecture.
concepts.example: Retrieving both a technical diagram and its surrounding text explanation to answer a question about a specific part.

concepts.eliForgot: Same four-step shape as text RAG, just done for pictures too: pull it out, turn it into numbers, file it away, then fetch it back.
concepts.definition: Ingestion (extract text and images from documents) → Embedding (convert text/images to vectors) → Indexing (store in a multimodal database) → Retrieval (unified retrieval of text and images).
concepts.example: Extracting both the paragraphs and the diagrams from a technical manual PDF, embedding each, and indexing them together for joint retrieval.

concepts.eliForgot: A model that tries to put pictures and captions describing them in the same neighborhood of vector space, so you can search across text and images together — though it doesn't always nail the alignment.
concepts.definition: A model used to embed diagrams/images for multimodal retrieval, alongside sentence transformers for text. A known challenge in multimodal RAG: CLIP vectors are not always semantically consistent with their paired text embeddings, which can hurt joint retrieval accuracy.
concepts.example: A CLIP embedding of a wiring diagram may not land as close, in vector space, to its text description as expected — an embedding-alignment issue.

concepts.eliForgot: A version of GPT-4 that can look at an image and read text at the same time, so it can answer a question using both.
concepts.definition: A multimodal LLM option that handles both text and image input, used in multimodal RAG to generate an integrated answer from retrieved text and images together.
concepts.example: A technician asks how to reset a safety sensor; multimodal RAG retrieves both the manual text and the relevant diagram, and GPT-4V generates an answer using both.

concepts.eliForgot: Adding images to RAG doesn't just add value, it adds new ways for the system to trip: mismatched embeddings, slower responses, fussier prompts, and evaluation that a script can't fully automate.
concepts.definition: Embedding alignment issues (CLIP vectors not always semantically consistent with text embeddings), latency concerns (slower processing for images), prompting complexity (formatting and tuning needed to combine modalities), and evaluation difficulties (human-in-the-loop needed since automated text metrics don't fully capture visual grounding quality).
concepts.example: Two teams building the same multimodal support bot both find that image-heavy queries are noticeably slower and harder to auto-evaluate than text-only ones.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between stemming and lemmatization?
flashcards.back: Stemming crudely chops suffixes (fast, sometimes produces non-words). Lemmatization uses linguistic rules to find the true dictionary base form (accurate, slower).

flashcards.front: Word2Vec: Skip-gram vs. CBOW — which predicts what?
flashcards.back: Skip-gram predicts context words from a target word (good for rare words). CBOW predicts the target word from context (faster, good for frequent words).

flashcards.front: Why does FastText handle out-of-vocabulary words better than Word2Vec?
flashcards.back: FastText represents words as character n-grams (subwords), so it can infer an embedding for an unseen word from its subword pieces.

flashcards.front: What does GloVe combine that Word2Vec doesn't?
flashcards.back: GloVe combines global corpus-wide co-occurrence statistics with local context; Word2Vec is purely local context-based.

flashcards.front: What's the main limitation of Bag of Words?
flashcards.back: It ignores word order and context entirely — "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce the same vector.

flashcards.front: Encoder-only vs. decoder-only vs. encoder-decoder: name the model for each.
flashcards.back: Encoder-only → BERT (understanding). Decoder-only → GPT (generation). Encoder-decoder → T5 (sequence-to-sequence).

flashcards.front: What are the three controllable inputs for reliable LLM output?
flashcards.back: Model, Parameters, and Prompt.

flashcards.front: What are the three core elements of an effective prompt?
flashcards.back: Clear instruction, context, and an output indicator.

flashcards.front: Chain-of-Thought vs. Tree-of-Thought — what's the key difference?
flashcards.back: CoT follows one linear reasoning chain. ToT branches into multiple reasoning paths, evaluates them, and converges on the best one.

flashcards.front: What's the main risk of Few-Shot Prompting?
flashcards.back: The order and choice of examples can greatly influence the outcome.

flashcards.front: Low temperature vs. high temperature — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Low temperature: factual Q&A, code generation, structured output. High temperature: creative writing, brainstorming.

flashcards.front: Top-k vs. top-p: fixed or adaptive cutoff?
flashcards.back: Top-k = fixed cutoff (always k tokens). Top-p (nucleus sampling) = adaptive cutoff (as many tokens as needed to hit the probability threshold).

flashcards.front: Frequency penalty vs. presence penalty — how do they differ?
flashcards.back: Frequency penalty scales with how many times a word has repeated. Presence penalty is a one-time flag just for appearing at all.

flashcards.front: In LangChain, what operator typically links runnables into a chain?
flashcards.back: The pipe operator `|`.

flashcards.front: What does Self-Consistency Prompting do differently from a single generation?
flashcards.back: It generates multiple answers to the same prompt and takes the majority/most consistent one, rather than trusting one run.

flashcards.front: What's the risk of ReAct / Action-Observation prompting?
flashcards.back: Increased complexity in prompt design, since it alternates reasoning and tool-based actions.

flashcards.front: Precision vs. Recall — in one line each.
flashcards.back: Precision: of what you flagged positive, how much was correct. Recall: of what was actually positive, how much did you catch.

flashcards.front: What's the F1 score formula?
flashcards.back: F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall) — the harmonic mean of the two.

flashcards.front: Why can accuracy be misleading?
flashcards.back: On an imbalanced dataset, always predicting the majority class can produce high accuracy while completely missing the minority class.

flashcards.front: Macro-average vs. weighted-average — which is better for imbalanced data?
flashcards.back: Weighted-average, since it accounts for class frequency; macro-average treats every class equally regardless of size.

flashcards.front: What's the key advantage of GenAI classification over traditional ML classification?
flashcards.back: No training data required (zero/few-shot), better handling of ambiguity/nuance, and it can provide explanations alongside predictions.

flashcards.front: What does a confusion matrix show that accuracy alone doesn't?
flashcards.back: Exactly which classes get mixed up with which other classes — not just the overall correct rate.

flashcards.front: Extractive vs. abstractive summarization — what's the core difference?
flashcards.back: Extractive pulls existing sentences directly from the source. Abstractive generates new sentences that paraphrase/synthesize the core ideas.

flashcards.front: What's the main limitation of ROUGE as a summarization metric?
flashcards.back: It measures lexical/n-gram overlap, so it doesn't account for semantic meaning or reward good paraphrasing.

flashcards.front: Why might BERTScore rate two summaries similarly even with almost no shared words?
flashcards.back: BERTScore compares embedding similarity (meaning), not exact word overlap, so it's robust to paraphrasing.

flashcards.front: Name the 5 summary rubric dimensions.
flashcards.back: Coverage, Coherence, Omission risk, Audience-appropriateness, Compression.

flashcards.front: What's a key limitation of extractive summarization?
flashcards.back: It can lack coherence when sentences are stitched together, and can't rephrase or abstract ideas — only reuse exact text.

flashcards.front: What's the biggest risk specific to abstractive summarization?
flashcards.back: Hallucinated content — since the model generates new text, it can introduce claims not actually in the source.

flashcards.front: What is the formula for Faithfulness?
flashcards.back: Faithfulness = (claims supported by sources) / (total claims in the response).

flashcards.front: Name the 5 types of hallucination.
flashcards.back: Intrinsic, Extrinsic, Compositional, Attribution errors, Continuity.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic hallucination?
flashcards.back: Intrinsic directly contradicts the source. Extrinsic adds claims that simply aren't present in the source at all.

flashcards.front: What's an 'attribution error' hallucination?
flashcards.back: The fact stated is correct, but it's attributed to the wrong source passage.

flashcards.front: Name the 5 QA rubric dimensions.
flashcards.back: Faithfulness/grounding, Factual correctness, Citation coverage, Answer completeness, Scope discipline.

flashcards.front: What is RAG?
flashcards.back: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — retrieving relevant context/documents and injecting them into the prompt before generation, to ground the answer in external knowledge.

flashcards.front: What penalty does BLEU apply, and why?
flashcards.back: A brevity penalty, to prevent the model from gaming the score by generating unnaturally short output.

flashcards.front: What's the key advantage of COMET over BLEU?
flashcards.back: COMET is a neural model trained on human judgments, so it aligns better with human perception of translation quality than pure n-gram overlap.

flashcards.front: Why does BLEU penalize good synonym-based translations?
flashcards.back: BLEU rewards exact n-gram overlap with the reference, so a correct translation using different words/synonyms scores lower even though it's accurate.

flashcards.front: When is Exact Match an appropriate metric, and when is it too strict?
flashcards.back: Appropriate for extractive QA or structured prediction with one fixed answer. Too strict for open-ended generation where many valid phrasings exist.

flashcards.front: What does pass@k measure?
flashcards.back: The probability that at least one of k sampled code completions passes all tests.

flashcards.front: pass@1 vs. pass@10 — which is stricter?
flashcards.back: pass@1 is stricter — the model gets only one attempt to be correct, vs. 10 chances for pass@10.

flashcards.front: What is a 'hallucinated API' failure mode?
flashcards.back: Generated code imports or calls methods/libraries that don't actually exist.

flashcards.front: Why is execution-based evaluation considered the strongest signal for code?
flashcards.back: It runs the code against real tests — pass/fail is a direct, unambiguous signal, no proxy metric needed.

flashcards.front: Name 3 standard code generation benchmarks.
flashcards.back: HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-Bench.

flashcards.front: What are the 4 stages of an end-to-end STT + summarization pipeline?
flashcards.back: Speech-to-Text conversion, text preprocessing, summarization, evaluation of the summary.

flashcards.front: Why is text preprocessing needed between STT and summarization?
flashcards.back: Raw transcriptions need cleaning and structuring for consistency before they're fed into a summarization step.

flashcards.front: What's the formula for Cohen's κ?
flashcards.back: κ = (P₀ − Pₑ) / (1 − Pₑ), where P₀ = observed agreement, Pₑ = agreement expected by chance.

flashcards.front: Cohen's κ = 0.70 — what agreement band is that?
flashcards.back: Substantial (0.61–0.80).

flashcards.front: Cohen's κ vs. Fleiss' κ — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Cohen's κ is for exactly two raters. Fleiss' κ extends it to three or more raters, and doesn't require the same raters for every item.

flashcards.front: When would you use Krippendorff's α instead of Cohen's or Fleiss' κ?
flashcards.back: When you have missing data, ordinal/interval/ratio scales (not just plain categories), or any number of raters — it's the most general but hardest to compute.

flashcards.front: Why does raw agreement (P₀) alone mislead you?
flashcards.back: It doesn't correct for chance — it inflates on skewed label distributions, since agreement can happen by accident when one label dominates.

flashcards.front: Name the 5 stages of the LLM workflow lifecycle.
flashcards.back: Ideation, Testing, Optimization, Evaluation, Monitoring.

flashcards.front: What are the 3 ways to use an LLM-as-a-judge?
flashcards.back: Pairwise Comparison, Numerical Scoring, Rubric-Based (most reliable).

flashcards.front: Name 3 biases that can mislead an LLM judge.
flashcards.back: Position bias, length bias, style bias (also: sycophancy, self-preference, confidence-fluency confusion).

flashcards.front: What correlation target should you aim for when calibrating an LLM judge against human scores?
flashcards.back: Pearson/Spearman correlation > 0.6.

flashcards.front: What does Evaluation-Driven Development (EDD) require you to do before writing a prompt?
flashcards.back: Define success criteria first and build an evaluation dataset — rubric comes before the prompt.

flashcards.front: What are the four axes for comparing models?
flashcards.back: Quality, Cost, Latency, Consistency.

flashcards.front: What makes a model 'Pareto-optimal'?
flashcards.back: No other model is both cheaper AND better than it.

flashcards.front: Why is stated model confidence unreliable as a correctness signal?
flashcards.back: Models can become systematically overconfident when self-reporting; self-consistency across multiple runs is a stronger signal.

flashcards.front: Low IAA on easy cases vs. low IAA on hard cases — what does each usually mean?
flashcards.back: Low IAA on easy cases = rubric is underspecified. Low IAA on hard cases only = usually expected, genuinely ambiguous data.

flashcards.front: What are the four output qualities that no single score captures together?
flashcards.back: Accuracy/Correctness, Relevance, Faithfulness, Confidence.

flashcards.front: What are the four DSPy primitives?
flashcards.back: Signatures, Modules, Metrics, Optimizers.

flashcards.front: What does a DSPy Signature declare?
flashcards.back: The interface: named inputs/outputs with their semantic purpose and type info — WHAT the program does, not HOW.

flashcards.front: Name 4 DSPy Modules.
flashcards.back: Predict, Chain-of-Thought, Program-of-Thought, ReAct.

flashcards.front: BootstrapFewShot vs. MIPROv2 — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: BootstrapFewShot: quick first win, limited budget, 10-50 examples. MIPROv2: maximum accuracy with budget available, 100+ examples, Bayesian joint search.

flashcards.front: What does GEPA stand for and how does it work?
flashcards.back: Genetic-Pareto — an evolutionary optimizer using natural language reflection to propose targeted prompt updates, keeping diverse top candidates to escape local maxima.

flashcards.front: In the DSPy paradigm shift, what do YOU actually engineer (instead of the prompt)?
flashcards.back: The specification (Signature), the metric, and the training data — the optimizer finds the actual prompt.

flashcards.front: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
flashcards.back: In deep/recurrent networks, gradients shrink as they backpropagate through many layers, making early weights barely update — crippling learning of long-range dependencies.

flashcards.front: What do Q, K, and V stand for in attention?
flashcards.back: Query (what we're looking for), Key (possible matches), Value (the actual information retrieved).

flashcards.front: What's the formula for scaled dot-product attention?
flashcards.back: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √dₖ) · V

flashcards.front: Why do we divide by √dₖ in scaled dot-product attention?
flashcards.back: To improve numerical stability for high-dimensional vectors — without scaling, dot products grow large and push softmax into low-gradient regions.

flashcards.front: What does multi-head attention let the model do that single-head self-attention can't?
flashcards.back: Focus on multiple different types of relationships simultaneously — each head learns a different relationship pattern, then outputs are concatenated.

flashcards.front: BERT's two pretraining tasks?
flashcards.back: Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP).

flashcards.front: Why is GPT called 'causal' or 'unidirectional'?
flashcards.back: It only attends to previous tokens (not future ones), since its job is predicting the next token given everything so far.

flashcards.front: What is T5's pretraining task called?
flashcards.back: Span Corruption — masking random spans of text and training the model to fill them in, similar in spirit to BERT's MLM.

flashcards.front: BERT-Base architecture specs?
flashcards.back: 12 layers, 768 hidden units, 12 attention heads.

flashcards.front: Why do positional embeddings matter in a Transformer?
flashcards.back: Attention has no inherent sense of word order, so positional embeddings add that information — otherwise 'John saw the dog' and 'The dog saw John' would look identical to the model.

flashcards.front: What's the core difference between how you work in Chat vs. Cowork?
flashcards.back: In Chat, you prompt, Claude responds, and you manually stitch outputs together. In Cowork, you define a task and Claude executes it as an agent end-to-end, reading and creating files directly.

flashcards.front: Match each Claude model tier to its best use: high-volume simple tasks, everyday business writing, complex multi-step strategy.
flashcards.back: Haiku → high-volume simple tasks (classification, extraction, routing). Sonnet → everyday business tasks (writing, analysis, daily workflows). Opus → complex reasoning, strategy, and multi-step analysis.

flashcards.front: Extended Thinking vs. Adaptive Thinking — who controls the reasoning depth in each?
flashcards.back: Extended Thinking: you explicitly set how much Claude should think (predictable token usage). Adaptive Thinking: Claude automatically scales reasoning based on detected complexity.

flashcards.front: What four elements should a well-structured system prompt define?
flashcards.back: Role (who Claude should be), Tone (how it communicates), Constraints (what to avoid), and Output Format (how the response should be structured).

flashcards.front: Name the four steps of the Agentic Loop in Cowork.
flashcards.back: Plan → Approve → Execute → Iterate: Claude announces the plan, the human approves it, Claude executes, and the human reviews/refines.

flashcards.front: What are the three human oversight mechanisms that make agentic AI safe for professional work?
flashcards.back: Visible Reasoning (Claude shows its thinking), Approval Gates (Claude asks before significant actions), and the Supervisor role (nothing happens without human sign-off).

flashcards.front: What's the difference between reusing prompts and reusing a Claude Skill?
flashcards.back: Reusing a prompt (Chat) means retyping instructions each time. A Skill (Cowork) saves an entire deterministic workflow so it can be triggered repeatedly with consistent output, and shared across a team.

flashcards.front: Why is 'no file upload needed' considered a marker of agentic behavior, not just a convenience?
flashcards.back: It means Claude is acting on local files directly and autonomously as part of executing a task, rather than only reacting to whatever content a user manually pastes or uploads into a chat message.

flashcards.front: What is RAG, in one sentence?
flashcards.back: An architecture that retrieves relevant external documents for a query, then has a generative model produce an answer grounded in that retrieved content, instead of relying only on trained-in knowledge.

flashcards.front: What are the two separate failure modes RAG is designed to fix?
flashcards.back: Generative-only: outdated info + hallucinations. Retrieval-only: no synthesis + user has to do the reading themselves.

flashcards.front: In the RAG = BERT + GPT framing, which model plays which role?
flashcards.back: BERT (bidirectional) plays the retriever — ranking/finding relevant text. GPT (unidirectional, left-to-right) plays the generator — writing the fluent answer.

flashcards.front: What does RAGAs evaluate, and at what level?
flashcards.back: The RAGAs framework evaluates a RAG pipeline at the component level: the Retriever Component (did it find the right context?) and the Generator Component (did it write a good answer from that context?) separately.

flashcards.front: What are the three primary levers for improving a RAG pipeline?
flashcards.back: Transform the data, transform the retrieval, transform the query.

flashcards.front: What are the four stages of a multimodal RAG pipeline?
flashcards.back: Ingestion (extract text + images) → Embedding (convert to vectors) → Indexing (store in a multimodal database) → Retrieval (unified retrieval of text and images).

flashcards.front: What embedding-related challenge is specific to multimodal RAG?
flashcards.back: Embedding alignment: CLIP vectors for images aren't always semantically consistent with the paired text embeddings, which can hurt joint retrieval accuracy.

flashcards.front: Why does multimodal RAG need human-in-the-loop evaluation more than text-only RAG?
flashcards.back: Because judging whether a retrieved diagram/image was actually the right visual grounding for the answer is harder to automate than text-based evaluation metrics.

quiz.question: Which technique breaks words into character n-grams to handle out-of-vocabulary words?
quiz.explanation: FastText represents words as character n-grams (subwords), allowing it to infer embeddings for unseen words.

quiz.question: A bigram is:
quiz.explanation: N-grams are contiguous sequences of n words; a bigram = 2 words (e.g. "The cat").

quiz.question: Which model architecture is decoder-only and built for text generation?
quiz.explanation: GPT consists only of decoder blocks with causal (unidirectional) attention, trained to predict the next token.

quiz.question: Why might you remove stop words before analysis?
options: To reduce noise and focus on meaningful terms
quiz.explanation: Stop words like "the" and "is" carry little semantic meaning; removing them reduces noise.

quiz.question: What core innovation let Transformers process text in parallel instead of sequentially like RNNs?
quiz.explanation: Attention lets the model weigh relationships between all tokens simultaneously, removing the need for sequential processing.

quiz.question: Which prompting technique has the model generate several answers and pick the majority result?
quiz.explanation: Self-Consistency Prompting produces several possible answers and seeks agreement/majority across them.

quiz.question: Which parameter puts a hard ceiling on output length regardless of content?
quiz.explanation: Max Tokens caps the output length by count; Stop Sequence caps it by pattern match.

quiz.question: In LangChain, what stores prompt text with `{}` placeholders for variables?
quiz.explanation: Prompt Templates hold the prompt text and placeholder variables, controlled by a Prompt Template object.

quiz.question: What's a caution specifically associated with Tree-of-Thought prompting?
options: Increased computation cost, more than Chain-of-Thought
quiz.explanation: ToT explores multiple branching reasoning paths, which costs more compute than CoT and requires designing merge/prune steps.

quiz.question: Which of the 7 generation parameters scales its penalty with how many times a word has already appeared?
quiz.explanation: Frequency Penalty penalizes proportional to the word's total count so far; Presence Penalty is a flat one-time penalty.

quiz.question: A spam filter flags 20 emails as spam; 15 actually are spam. What is its precision?
quiz.explanation: Precision = correctly predicted positives / all predicted positives = 15/20 = 0.75.

quiz.question: Which metric is the harmonic mean of precision and recall?
quiz.explanation: F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall).

quiz.question: In a dataset that's 95% one label, why is accuracy alone a poor metric?
options: Accuracy can't be computed on imbalanced data
A model can score 95% just by always predicting the majority class
quiz.explanation: Class imbalance inflates accuracy since the majority-class heuristic alone achieves a high score without real discrimination.

quiz.question: What is a key benefit of using GenAI (LLMs) for classification over traditional supervised ML?
options: It requires more labeled training data
It can work in zero- or few-shot settings and handle nuance/ambiguity better
It removes the need for evaluation
quiz.explanation: LLMs can classify without training data and handle ambiguity/context better, though they introduce stochasticity that traditional models don't have.

quiz.question: Aspect-Based Sentiment Classification (ABSC) differs from standard sentiment analysis by:
options: Assigning sentiment to specific aspects/attributes within the text, not just overall
quiz.explanation: ABSC breaks sentiment down per aspect (e.g. battery life vs. camera) rather than giving one overall sentiment label.

quiz.question: Which summarization approach directly pulls sentences from the source text without rewriting them?
quiz.explanation: Extractive summarization identifies and pulls key sentences/phrases directly, without generating new text.

quiz.question: Why is BERTScore generally better than ROUGE at rewarding a good paraphrase?
options: BERTScore compares embedding-based semantic similarity, not just word overlap
quiz.explanation: BERTScore uses embeddings to measure meaning similarity, so paraphrased text scores well even with different wording.

quiz.question: A summary is well-written and covers all key points but was written for executives when the audience needed operational detail. Which rubric dimension does this fail?
quiz.explanation: Audience-appropriateness is specifically about matching the level of detail to the reader's needs.

quiz.question: What is the primary risk of abstractive summarization compared to extractive?
options: It's always more expensive to run
Risk of generating inaccurate or hallucinated content
quiz.explanation: Because abstractive summarization generates new text, it risks fabricating content not present in the source.

quiz.question: ROUGE-L specifically measures overlap based on:
quiz.explanation: ROUGE-L captures sequence-level overlap via the longest common subsequence between candidate and reference.

quiz.question: A response makes 8 factual claims; 6 are supported by the source document. What is its faithfulness score?
quiz.explanation: Faithfulness = supported claims / total claims = 6/8 = 0.75.

quiz.question: A model states a true fact but cites the wrong source passage for it. This is which hallucination type?
quiz.explanation: Attribution errors are correct facts attributed to the wrong source.

quiz.question: Which QA failure mode describes answering only half of a multi-part question?
quiz.explanation: A partial answer addresses only part of the question asked.

quiz.question: What does 'scope discipline' mean in QA evaluation?
options: The model answers as fast as possible
The model provides no information beyond what was actually asked
The model uses a fixed vocabulary
quiz.explanation: Scope discipline means not overreaching beyond the actual question asked.

quiz.question: Which hallucination type involves combining true individual facts into a false overall conclusion?
quiz.explanation: Compositional hallucination: true facts → false conclusion when combined incorrectly.

quiz.question: BLEU is best described as measuring:
options: N-gram precision with a brevity penalty
quiz.explanation: BLEU measures n-gram precision between candidate and reference text, with a brevity penalty against overly short outputs.

quiz.question: Which metric is trained directly on human judgments of translation quality?
quiz.explanation: COMET is a neural evaluation model trained on human judgments, aligning better with perceived adequacy and fluency.

quiz.question: A reference and output convey the same meaning using totally different words. A lexical metric will likely score this:
options: Low, since word overlap is low
quiz.explanation: Lexical metrics reward surface word overlap, not meaning, so a good paraphrase scores low despite being correct.

quiz.question: A model is evaluated with pass@1 = 30% and pass@10 = 65%. What does this tell you?
options: Given 10 attempts, correct code appears far more often than with a single attempt
pass@10 is always lower than pass@1
quiz.explanation: pass@k increases with k since more sampled attempts increase the chance at least one is fully correct.

quiz.question: Generated code imports a function that has never existed in the library. This is:
quiz.explanation: Hallucinated APIs are imports or methods that don't actually exist in the real library.

quiz.question: What is the strongest evaluation signal for whether generated code is correct?
options: Execution-based evaluation (running it against a test harness)
quiz.explanation: Running the code against real tests gives a direct pass/fail signal — no proxy metric needed.

quiz.question: Code that was correct for an old version of a library but breaks with the current version is an example of:
quiz.explanation: Version drift occurs when generated code reflects an outdated API that has since changed.

quiz.question: In an STT + summarization pipeline, what comes immediately after transcription?
quiz.explanation: The pipeline is: STT → text preprocessing (cleaning/structuring) → summarization → evaluation.

quiz.question: Which evaluation methods are suggested for the summarization stage of this pipeline?
quiz.explanation: The pipeline explicitly names ROUGE and LLM eval as evaluation methods for the summarization output.

quiz.question: Two raters agree on 85 of 100 items. Given P(A=+)=0.55, P(B=+)=0.50, P(A=−)=0.45, P(B=−)=0.50, what is Cohen's κ?
Which IAA metric should you use with 3+ raters who rotate through a pool of examples (not the same raters every time)?
quiz.explanation: Fleiss' κ extends Cohen's κ to 3+ raters and doesn't require the same raters for every item.

quiz.question: An LLM judge, when shown option A first and then B, prefers A. When the order is reversed, it now prefers B. This demonstrates:
quiz.explanation: Position bias is when the first-presented option in a pairwise comparison is favored regardless of actual quality.

quiz.question: In Evaluation-Driven Development, what comes first?
options: Defining success criteria and building the evaluation dataset
quiz.explanation: EDD's core principle: rubric comes first, prompt comes second — you cannot improve what you haven't defined.

quiz.question: A model is Pareto-optimal if:
options: It has the highest quality score of all models
It is the cheapest model available
No other model is both cheaper and better
quiz.explanation: Pareto-optimality means no other model dominates it on both cost and quality simultaneously.

quiz.question: What should you do BEFORE trusting a gold-standard evaluation dataset?
options: Run only automated metrics on it
quiz.explanation: IAA should be measured before trusting the dataset, not after training/evaluating on it — low IAA signals the gold set itself may be unreliable.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the 5 stages of the LLM workflow lifecycle?
quiz.explanation: The 5 stages are Ideation, Testing, Optimization, Evaluation, Monitoring. Tokenization is a preprocessing step, not a lifecycle stage.

quiz.question: Why is stated LLM confidence considered an unreliable signal on its own?
options: It can become systematically overconfident and doesn't reliably track actual correctness
It only applies to classification tasks
quiz.explanation: Self-reported confidence is unreliable on its own; self-consistency across multiple independent runs is a stronger signal.

quiz.question: Which DSPy primitive declares named inputs/outputs without dictating the exact prompt wording?
quiz.explanation: Signatures declare the interface (what), separating it from the mechanics (how) — optimizers rewrite the prompt while preserving the contract.

quiz.question: A team has only 15 labeled examples and a very limited budget. Which optimizer should they start with?
quiz.explanation: BootstrapFewShot is the quick, low-cost first win, appropriate for 10-50 examples.

quiz.question: Which DSPy Module alternates between reasoning and taking actions like tool calls?
quiz.explanation: ReAct alternates reasoning and action, calling tools and observing results before continuing to reason.

quiz.question: In DSPy, what tells the optimizer whether one candidate prompt is 'better' than another?
quiz.explanation: Metrics return a score that guides the optimizer's search toward better-performing candidates.

quiz.question: What core limitation of RNNs directly motivated the invention of the Transformer?
quiz.explanation: RNNs' vanishing/exploding gradients and inability to parallelize (sequential bottleneck) directly motivated the Transformer's attention-based, parallelizable design.

quiz.question: In scaled dot-product attention, what is divided by √dₖ before applying softmax?
options: The dot product of Query and Key
quiz.explanation: The QKᵀ dot product is scaled by √dₖ for numerical stability before softmax is applied.

quiz.question: Which model is encoder-only and best suited for classification and extractive QA?
quiz.explanation: BERT is encoder-only, using bidirectional attention, purpose-built for understanding tasks.

quiz.question: T5's core design philosophy is that:
options: Every NLP task should be reframed as text-to-text
quiz.explanation: T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) reframes every task, from classification to translation, as a text-to-text problem.

quiz.question: Why does GPT use unidirectional (causal) attention instead of bidirectional?
options: Its task is next-token prediction, so it must not see future tokens
quiz.explanation: As a causal language model, GPT predicts the next token from only the preceding context, so it can't attend to future tokens without leaking the answer.

quiz.question: Multi-head attention improves on single-head self-attention primarily by:
options: Letting different heads learn different types of relationships in parallel
Removing the need for positional embeddings
quiz.explanation: Each attention head has its own Q/K/V matrices and can specialize in different relationship types (e.g. subject-verb vs. object-preposition), improving expressiveness.

quiz.question: Which Claude ecosystem layer is best suited for a one-off task like rewriting a paragraph for tone?
quiz.explanation: Chat is built for quick, one-off tasks with a clear start and end — exactly the 'AI as consultant' use case.

quiz.question: A task needs the cheapest, fastest model for classifying thousands of support tickets. Which tier fits best?
quiz.explanation: Haiku is optimized for speed and scale on high-volume, simple tasks like classification and routing.

quiz.question: In the Agentic Loop, what happens in the 'Approve' step?
options: Claude reads files and starts generating output immediately
The human reviews Claude's proposed plan before any work begins
Claude schedules the task to run automatically next month
The human edits the output directly in the file
quiz.explanation: Approve sits between Plan and Execute: the human reviews the plan and signs off before Claude starts doing the work.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four elements a Claude system prompt should define?
quiz.explanation: System prompt design covers Role, Tone, Constraints, and Output Format. Temperature is a generation parameter, not a system prompt element.

quiz.question: What distinguishes Sub-Agent Coordination from simply asking Claude one question at a time?
options: It requires uploading every file manually
It breaks complex work into smaller tasks handled as parallel workstreams
It only works inside Claude Chat
It replaces the need for an approval gate
quiz.explanation: Sub-agent coordination splits a complex task into smaller pieces worked on in parallel, rather than processing everything sequentially in one thread.

quiz.question: What does CLAUDE.md primarily provide in a Cowork workflow?
options: A one-time prompt template used only for the first task
Persistent project context (conventions, targets, rules) that loads automatically every session
A log of completed tasks for billing purposes
The system prompt's temperature and max token settings
quiz.explanation: CLAUDE.md holds standing project context — folder conventions, KPI targets, thresholds, and workflow rules — that Claude loads automatically each session instead of being re-briefed.

quiz.question: A retrieval-only search engine and a generative-only LLM are each given the query "What happens in a breach of contract?" What's the key difference in their failure modes?
options: The retrieval-only system hallucinates; the generative-only system fails to synthesize
The retrieval-only system returns unsynthesized source lists (user must read them); the generative-only system may hallucinate or be outdated
Both systems fail identically because neither can access legal documents
The retrieval-only system is always more accurate than the generative-only system
quiz.explanation: Retrieval-only systems lack synthesis and place the burden on the user to review sources; generative-only models lack up-to-date info and are prone to hallucination — these are two distinct failure modes, which is exactly why RAG combines both.

quiz.question: In the "RAG = BERT-like retrieval + GPT-like generation" framing, which statement is accurate?
options: BERT is unidirectional and excels at fluent generation
GPT is bidirectional and excels at document ranking
BERT is bidirectional and strong at retrieval/ranking; GPT is unidirectional (left-to-right) and strong at fluent generation
Both BERT and GPT are equally strong at both retrieval and generation
quiz.explanation: BERT's bidirectional context understanding makes it well-suited to retrieval, ranking, and QA, but it can't generate fluent responses. GPT's unidirectional, left-to-right modeling makes it fluent but prone to hallucination without retrieval.

quiz.question: What does the RAGAs framework specifically let you evaluate that a single end-to-end "is the final answer good?" score does not?
options: The exact token cost of each generation call
The Retriever and Generator components of the RAG pipeline separately, so you can tell whether retrieval or generation is the actual problem
Whether the underlying LLM was fine-tuned or prompted
The latency of the vector database only
quiz.explanation: RAGAs evaluates a RAG pipeline at the component level — the Retriever Component and the Generator Component — so failures can be attributed to the right stage instead of judging only the final output.

quiz.question: A team's RAG chatbot keeps giving good answers to well-phrased questions but poor answers to vague or ambiguous user questions. Which of the three levers for improving RAG most directly targets this problem?
quiz.explanation: Query transformation rewrites or expands the user's query before retrieval — the most direct lever when the problem traces back to how the question itself was phrased, as opposed to what's indexed or how ranking works.

quiz.question: A technician asks a multimodal RAG system, "How do I reset the safety sensor?" Why might a traditional (text-only) RAG system fail here where multimodal RAG succeeds?
options: Traditional RAG cannot process any text queries about hardware
Traditional RAG retrieves the relevant text but misses a critical diagram that the answer depends on
Multimodal RAG doesn't use an LLM at all, only image matching
Traditional RAG is always slower than multimodal RAG
quiz.explanation: Traditional RAG retrieves text chunks only, so it misses information that lives in a diagram or schematic. Multimodal RAG retrieves both the text and the diagram, letting a model like GPT-4V generate an answer grounded in both.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a documented challenge specific to multimodal RAG (beyond the challenges of text-only RAG)?
options: CLIP-based image embeddings are not always semantically consistent with paired text embeddings
LLMs cannot process any image data under any circumstances
Multimodal RAG eliminates the need for an indexing step entirely
Multimodal RAG requires no evaluation since images are self-explanatory
quiz.explanation: Embedding alignment is a named challenge: CLIP vectors for images aren't always semantically consistent with text embeddings, alongside latency, prompting complexity, and the need for human-in-the-loop evaluation.
